## Anomaly Localization

**Implicated nodes:** `i_1` (199, accumulated reward), `i_2` (10, fee percent), `i_3` (100, percent denominator), `op_1` (divide: i_1 / i_3 → o_4), `o_4` (reported = 1), `op_2` (multiply: o_4 * i_2 → o_5), `o_5` (reported = 10, "Developer reward (fee)").

**Flow:** The pipeline computes the developer fee as `(reward / denominator) * percent` instead of the mathematically equivalent `(reward * percent) / denominator`. Because every variable in this graph is typed `java.math.BigInteger` — an integer type with no fractional component and no `MathContext`/rounding-mode argument at all — the division in `op_1` is a **floor/truncating integer division that is performed before the multiplication that would have preserved the lost precision**.

- `op_1`: `199 / 100` → exact rational value is `1.99`; BigInteger truncates to `1`. This step alone discards `0.99` (≈50% of the value that flows into the next operation).
- `op_2`: `1 * 10 = 10` is then reported as the developer fee.

Had the operations been ordered as multiply-then-divide (the standard-safe order for percentage math), the computation would have been `199 * 10 = 1990`, then `1990 / 100 = 19` (still integer-truncated, but far closer to the exact fee of `19.9`). The reported result of `10` versus the correctly-ordered result of `19` is a **Δ of 9 units on a base fee of ~19–20**, i.e. roughly a 47–50% understatement of the fee — not a 1-ULP rounding artifact.

## Details

**Mechanism:** This is a textbook premature-division precision defect. Dividing `i_1` by `i_3` first collapses the fractional remainder (`0.99` out of `1.99`) into an integer BigInteger truncation to `1`, irreversibly discarding ~50% of the value that should have propagated into the fee calculation. Multiplying afterward by the fee percent (`i_2`) cannot recover that lost fraction — it merely scales the already-truncated intermediate. This is precisely the "reducing an intermediate value's scale before completing an aggregation" pattern called out in the invariant definition, and it is why a naive dependency/type check passes: every node is internally type-consistent (`BigInteger` throughout, correctly wired arguments, no duplicate/reused IDs), so structural heuristics see nothing wrong. Only recomputing the exact rational arithmetic and comparing operation *order* against the standard-safe convention (multiply before divide when working in integer domains) exposes the flaw.

**Why this clears the materiality bar (not mere rounding-mode ambiguity):** The invariant explicitly states that a single truncate-vs-round difference can differ by at most 1 unit at the target scale. Here the discrepancy is 9 units out of an expected ~19-20 — nearly an order of magnitude beyond what any legitimate rounding-mode choice (HALF_UP, HALF_EVEN, FLOOR, etc.) could produce on its own. This is not "wrong rounding mode," it is wrong **operation order** causing structural information loss, which the invariants treat as a materiality override regardless of whether this is a one-off calculation.

**Cyclic/scalable context:** The descriptor ("Staking: developer fee deduction") indicates this formula executes on every reward distribution across a staking pool — a population that scales with the number of stakers, epochs, and reward events. Even though this single trace shows one occurrence, the underlying operation pattern is inherently repeatable at high frequency, meaning the value leakage (in this instance, benefiting whichever side retains the undeducted remainder — the staker receives `189` instead of the correct `~180`) compounds systematically rather than being a bounded, one-time event. This satisfies the "scalable operation population" criterion for elevated risk, independent of the single-trace materiality already found.

**Impact:** The developer fee is understated by roughly half of its correct value on this trace, and the underlying operation-order defect will reproduce this understatement on every future execution of this fee-deduction routine, systematically diverting value away from the intended fee recipient at scale.
